verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — A Sword for a Razor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel shaves his head and beard with a sword and weighs the hair into three parts: a third burned in the model city, a third struck with the sword, a third scattered to the wind (vv. 1-2). A few hairs are tucked into his robe, and even some of those are thrown into the fire (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment will fall on all, and even the preserved remnant is not safe apart from God's mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, O son of man, take a sharp sword. Use it as a barber's razor and pass it over your head and your beard. Then take balances for weighing and divide the hair. A third part you shall burn in the fire in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are completed. And a third part you shall take and strike with the sword all around the city. And a third part you shall scatter to the wind, and I will unsheathe the sword after them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And you, O son of man, take a sharp sword. Use it as a barber's razor and pass it over your head and your beard. Then take balances for weighing and divide the hair.

A sword as a razor — the instrument of war used for a barber's job. Ezekiel shaves off his hair and his beard.

For a priest, this was shocking. The law said priests shall not make bald patches on their heads, nor shave off the edges of their beards (Lev 21:5). And a shaved beard was a public humiliation: when an enemy king wanted to disgrace David's envoys, he shaved off half the beard of each (2 Sam 10:4). Isaiah had warned that the Lord would shave Judah with a razor that is hired beyond the River (Isa 7:20). Babylon is that razor, and the sword in Ezekiel's hand says so.

A third part you shall burn in the fire in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are completed. And a third part you shall take and strike with the sword all around the city. And a third part you shall scatter to the wind, and I will unsheathe the sword after them.

The hair is weighed out on scales: judgment is exact. One third burned inside the city, one third cut down around it, one third blown away — and even the scattered third is chased by a drawn sword. Verse 12 will explain: pestilence and famine inside, the sword outside, exile and pursuit beyond.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall take from these a small number and bind them in the skirts of your robe. And of these again you shall take some and cast them into the midst of the fire and burn them in the fire. From there a fire will come out into all the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you shall take from these a small number and bind them in the skirts of your robe.

A few hairs are saved, tucked into the fold of his robe. Here is the remnant: a small number that God keeps.

And of these again you shall take some and cast them into the midst of the fire and burn them in the fire. From there a fire will come out into all the house of Israel.

But even some of the saved hairs go into the fire. Being among the survivors was no guarantee. Some who escaped the siege would still perish; even in exile, judgment would continue to fall on those who did not turn.

That is a sobering word to anyone who thinks being in the right group is enough. Outward membership in God's people does not save. Only a living relationship with God does. And the remnant that is truly kept is kept by God's hand, not its own strength.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–17 — I, Even I, Am Against You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is Jerusalem, set in the centre of the nations (v. 5), yet more wicked than the nations around her (vv. 6-7). So God says Behold, I, even I, am against you (v. 8), and he will do what he has never done before (v. 9). Parents and children will eat each other (v. 10); because she defiled his sanctuary, his eye will not spare (v. 11). Pestilence, sword and scattering will take her in thirds (v. 12) until his fury is spent and they shall know that I am the LORD (v. 13). She will become a reproach and a warning among the nations, under the arrows of famine, wild beasts, plague and sword (vv. 14-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The greater the privilege of God's people, the greater the judgment when they despise it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: This is Jerusalem. I have set her in the center of the nations, with countries all around her. And she has rebelled against my rules by doing wickedness more than the nations, and against my statutes more than the countries all around her; for they have rejected my rules and have not walked in my statutes. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you are more turbulent than the nations that are all around you, and have not walked in my statutes or obeyed my rules, and have not even acted according to the rules of the nations that are all around you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the Lord GOD: This is Jerusalem. I have set her in the center of the nations, with countries all around her.

Three words that interpret everything: This is Jerusalem. The hair, the brick, the siege — all of it is about the holy city.

And God says why her guilt is so great. I have set her in the center of the nations. Jerusalem was placed where the world could see her, meant to be a showcase of what life under God looks like. Moses had said that the nations, seeing Israel's laws, would say Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people (Deut 4:6). God's people were always meant to be a light for the nations (Isa 49:6).

And she has rebelled against my rules by doing wickedness more than the nations, and against my statutes more than the countries all around her; for they have rejected my rules and have not walked in my statutes.

Instead of being a light, she became darker than the darkness around her. The city with the law behaved worse than the cities without it.

Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you are more turbulent than the nations that are all around you, and have not walked in my statutes or obeyed my rules, and have not even acted according to the rules of the nations that are all around you,

Not even as good as the pagans. (The ESV notes that some manuscripts lack not, which would make the charge: you have acted just like the nations. Either reading condemns her.)

Paul makes the same charge against those who have God's law but break it: The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you (Rom 2:24). When the church lives worse than the world, the world does not only see hypocrites; it thinks less of God.

verseByVerse.quote: therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I, even I, am against you. And I will execute judgments in your midst in the sight of the nations. And because of all your abominations I will do with you what I have never yet done, and the like of which I will never do again. Therefore fathers shall eat their sons in your midst, and sons shall eat their fathers. And I will execute judgments on you, and any of you who survive I will scatter to all the winds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I, even I, am against you. And I will execute judgments in your midst in the sight of the nations.

I, even I, am against you. It is a fearful thing to hear from God. Not Babylon against you; God against you.

And there is a play on words the ESV notes explain: the same Hebrew expression can mean "obey rules" or "execute judgments". Jerusalem would not obey my rules (v. 7); so God will execute judgments. The rules they would not keep become the judgments they cannot escape. And it will happen in the sight of the nations, the same nations who were supposed to see her obedience.

And because of all your abominations I will do with you what I have never yet done, and the like of which I will never do again.

God himself says this judgment will stand alone. Jesus used similar language of the city's later destruction: great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now (Matt 24:21).

Therefore fathers shall eat their sons in your midst, and sons shall eat their fathers. And I will execute judgments on you, and any of you who survive I will scatter to all the winds.

The worst horror of siege, foretold in the covenant curses (Lev 26:29) and mourned in Lamentations (Lam 4:10). Sin unmakes the family itself.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as I live, declares the Lord GOD, surely, because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your detestable things and with all your abominations, therefore I will withdraw. My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity. A third part of you shall die of pestilence and be consumed with famine in your midst; a third part shall fall by the sword all around you; and a third part I will scatter to all the winds and will unsheathe the sword after them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, as I live, declares the Lord GOD, surely, because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your detestable things and with all your abominations, therefore I will withdraw. My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity.

Here is the heart of the charge: you have defiled my sanctuary. Chapter 8 will show Ezekiel exactly what they did inside the temple. The holiest place on earth had been filled with idols.

So I will withdraw. (The ESV notes that some manuscripts read "I will cut you down".) God pulls back his protecting presence. Chapters 10-11 will show the glory actually leaving.

My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity. God is compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. But his patience is not endless for those who treat his holiness with contempt. Do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? (Rom 2:4).

A third part of you shall die of pestilence and be consumed with famine in your midst; a third part shall fall by the sword all around you; and a third part I will scatter to all the winds and will unsheathe the sword after them.

Now the hair of verses 1-2 is explained, third by third. The sign was not theatre. It was a map of what was coming.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus shall my anger spend itself, and I will vent my fury upon them and satisfy myself. And they shall know that I am the LORD—that I have spoken in my jealousy— when I spend my fury upon them. Moreover, I will make you a desolation and an object of reproach among the nations all around you and in the sight of all who pass by. You shall be a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror, to the nations all around you, when I execute judgments on you in anger and fury, and with furious rebukes—I am the LORD; I have spoken—
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus shall my anger spend itself, and I will vent my fury upon them and satisfy myself. And they shall know that I am the LORD—that I have spoken in my jealousy— when I spend my fury upon them.

My anger spend itself... and satisfy myself. God's wrath is not an endless rage; it is a just response that comes to an end when justice is done. That is why the gospel speaks of Christ as a propitiation by his blood (Rom 3:25): God's just anger against sin was fully spent on his Son, so that nothing is left over for those who trust him.

In my jealousy. God's jealousy is not petty envy. It is the burning love of a husband whose wife has gone after other lovers. He will not share his people with idols, because idols destroy them.

And the purpose: they shall know that I am the LORD. This sentence, in one form or another, comes some seventy times in Ezekiel. It is the goal of everything God does in this book — judgment and restoration alike. People who would not know God through his kindness will come to know him through his judgments. Far better to know him the other way.

Moreover, I will make you a desolation and an object of reproach among the nations all around you and in the sight of all who pass by.

You shall be a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror, to the nations all around you, when I execute judgments on you in anger and fury, and with furious rebukes—I am the LORD; I have spoken—

Jerusalem was meant to be a showcase; now she becomes a warning. People will point at her ruins and learn what it means to despise God. Her story is still a warning: these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction (1 Cor 10:11).

verseByVerse.quote: when I send against you the deadly arrows of famine, arrows for destruction, which I will send to destroy you, and when I bring more and more famine upon you and break your supply of bread. I will send famine and wild beasts against you, and they will rob you of your children. Pestilence and blood shall pass through you, and I will bring the sword upon you. I am the LORD; I have spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
when I send against you the deadly arrows of famine, arrows for destruction, which I will send to destroy you, and when I bring more and more famine upon you and break your supply of bread.

I will send famine and wild beasts against you, and they will rob you of your children. Pestilence and blood shall pass through you, and I will bring the sword upon you. I am the LORD; I have spoken."

Famine, wild beasts, pestilence, sword — the covenant curses listed long before. Moses had heard God say I will spend my arrows on them; they shall be wasted with hunger, and devoured by plague (Deut 32:23-24). (The ESV notes that supply is "staff" again, as in 4:16.)

And the chapter ends as a signature: I am the LORD; I have spoken. That is the guarantee. Every word of warning in the Bible stands on it. And so does every word of promise. The same God who said I have spoken about the siege will say it about the new heart and the new spirit (36:36). What he says, he does.

5.title: This Is Jerusalem
5.overview:
Ezekiel shaves his head and beard with a sword, weighs the hair and divides it into three parts: a third burned in the city, a third struck with the sword around it, and a third scattered to the wind with a sword pursuing. A few hairs are bound in his robe, and some of those are thrown into the fire (vv. 1-4).

God explains: this is Jerusalem. He set her in the centre of the nations, but she has rebelled against his rules more than the nations around her. So God himself is against her. He will do what he has never done before; parents and children will eat each other; because she has defiled his sanctuary, he will withdraw and have no pity (vv. 5-11).

A third will die of pestilence and famine, a third by the sword, and a third will be scattered and pursued. His anger will be spent, and they will know that he is the LORD who spoke in his jealousy. Jerusalem will become a desolation, a reproach and a warning to the nations, under the arrows of famine, wild beasts, pestilence and the sword. I am the LORD; I have spoken (vv. 12-17).
5.theology:
God's judgment is exact and complete, and even among survivors only those God truly keeps are safe (vv. 1-4).

Privilege increases accountability: Jerusalem, set before the nations to display God's ways, was judged for being worse than they (vv. 5-7; Deut 4:6-8; Rom 2:24).

The rules God's people will not keep become the judgments they cannot escape (vv. 7-8).

Defiling God's holiness provokes his withdrawal (v. 11; Rom 2:4).

God's wrath is just and comes to an end when it is satisfied; in Christ it has been fully spent (v. 13; Rom 3:25).

The goal of God's acts is that people know he is the LORD (v. 13), and his spoken word guarantees both judgment and promise (v. 17; 36:36).
5.examples:
A priest shaving his beard with a sword.

Hair weighed on scales.

A few hairs tucked into a robe, and some of them still burned.

A city set in the shop window of the world.

The rules you would not keep becoming the judgments you cannot escape.

I am the LORD; I have spoken.

Thus says the Lord GOD to the mountains and the hills, to the ravines and the valleys: Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places.<sup>4</sup>Your altars shall become desolate, and your incense altars shall be broken, and I will cast down your slain before your idols.<sup>5</sup>And I will lay the dead bodies of the people of Israel before their idols, and I will scatter your bones around your altars.<sup>6</sup>Wherever you dwell, the cities shall be waste and the high places ruined, so that your altars will be waste and ruined, your idols broken and destroyed, your incense altars cut down, and your works wiped out.<sup>7</sup>And the slain shall fall in your midst, and you shall know that I am the LORD.<sup>8</sup>"Yet I will leave some of you alive. When you have among the nations some who escape the sword, and when you are scattered through the countries,<sup>9</sup>then those of you who escape will remember me among the nations where they are carried captive, how I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me and over their eyes that go whoring after their idols. And they will be loathsome in their own sight for the evils that they have committed, for all their abominations.<sup>10</sup>And they shall know that I am the LORD. I have not said in vain that I would do this evil to them."<sup>11</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD: "Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Alas, because of all the evil abominations of the house of Israel, for they shall fall by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence.<sup>12</sup>He who is far off shall die of pestilence, and he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who is left and is preserved shall die of famine. Thus I will spend my fury upon them.<sup>13</sup>And you shall know that I am the LORD, when their slain lie among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the mountaintops, under every green tree, and under every leafy oak, wherever they offered pleasing aroma to all their idols.<sup>14</sup>And I will stretch out my hand against them and make the land desolate and waste, in all their dwelling places, from the wilderness to Riblah. Then they will know that I am the LORD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel turns his face toward the mountains of Israel, where the high places stood (vv. 1-3). God will bring the sword on them, break their altars and lay the bodies of his people in front of their idols, scattering their bones around the altars (vv. 4-5). Every city will be waste and every idol smashed (v. 6), and you shall know that I am the LORD (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The false gods people trust will lie broken beside those who trusted them.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them, and say, You mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD! Thus says the Lord GOD to the mountains and the hills, to the ravines and the valleys: Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to me:

"Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them,

Ezekiel is in Babylon, but he is told to turn and face the hills of home. Picture him staring westward across the desert and speaking to mountains hundreds of miles away. The word of God is not limited by distance.

and say, You mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD! Thus says the Lord GOD to the mountains and the hills, to the ravines and the valleys: Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places.

Why speak to mountains? Because that is where the idolatry happened. The high places were hilltop shrines where Israel worshipped other gods, or worshipped the LORD in pagan ways. God had commanded them at the beginning to destroy all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods, on the high mountains and on the hills and under every green tree (Deut 12:2). Instead Israel took them over.

The land itself is addressed as a witness and a defendant. The mountains, the ravines and the valleys had seen everything.

And remember that the promise will come to the same mountains. In chapter 36 God will say, But you, O mountains of Israel, shall shoot forth your branches and yield your fruit to my people Israel (36:8). The hills that are cursed here will be blessed there.

verseByVerse.quote: Your altars shall become desolate, and your incense altars shall be broken, and I will cast down your slain before your idols. And I will lay the dead bodies of the people of Israel before their idols, and I will scatter your bones around your altars. Wherever you dwell, the cities shall be waste and the high places ruined, so that your altars will be waste and ruined, your idols broken and destroyed, your incense altars cut down, and your works wiped out. And the slain shall fall in your midst, and you shall know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your altars shall become desolate, and your incense altars shall be broken, and I will cast down your slain before your idols.

And I will lay the dead bodies of the people of Israel before their idols, and I will scatter your bones around your altars.

A grim picture, and a deliberate one. The worshippers will lie dead in front of the gods they worshipped. The idols will look on and do nothing, because they can do nothing. They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see... Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps 115:5, 8).

Dead bodies and bones made a place unclean. The altars they thought were holy will be defiled with the corpses of the people who served there.

Wherever you dwell, the cities shall be waste and the high places ruined, so that your altars will be waste and ruined, your idols broken and destroyed, your incense altars cut down, and your works wiped out.

The ESV notes that ruined may also be "punished". And the list goes on piling up the ruin: waste, ruined, broken, destroyed, cut down, wiped out. Your works — everything they made with their own hands to replace God.

That is always the end of idolatry, ancient or modern. Whatever we build to trust instead of God — careers, reputations, relationships, comforts — cannot hold our weight in the day of trouble, and will be broken.

And the slain shall fall in your midst, and you shall know that I am the LORD.

Here is the refrain again. They would not know God as the LORD when he gave them the land and every good gift. They will know him when their idols lie in pieces.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — Broken over Their Whoring Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Yet I will leave some of you alive (v. 8). Among the nations the survivors will remember God, how I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me, and they will loathe themselves for their evils (v. 9). They will know that God did not speak in vain (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: God grieves over his people's unfaithfulness, and true repentance begins when they see their sin as he sees it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet I will leave some of you alive. When you have among the nations some who escape the sword, and when you are scattered through the countries, then those of you who escape will remember me among the nations where they are carried captive, how I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me and over their eyes that go whoring after their idols. And they will be loathsome in their own sight for the evils that they have committed, for all their abominations. And they shall know that I am the LORD. I have not said in vain that I would do this evil to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Yet I will leave some of you alive. When you have among the nations some who escape the sword, and when you are scattered through the countries,

After seven verses of destruction, one word changes the tone: Yet. God will leave a remnant. Judgment is never God's final word to his people.

then those of you who escape will remember me among the nations where they are carried captive, how I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me and over their eyes that go whoring after their idols. And they will be loathsome in their own sight for the evils that they have committed, for all their abominations.

Read slowly. How I have been broken over their whoring heart. God says he is broken. The Lord of the storm and the fire (chapter 1), who is sending sword and famine, speaks like a betrayed husband whose heart has been crushed.

This is a tender glimpse of God's heart. It stands with it grieved him to his heart (Gen 6:6), and with Jesus weeping over Jerusalem: How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! (Matt 23:37). God's judgment does not come from a cold heart. Sin is not only law-breaking; it breaks his heart. Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God (Eph 4:30).

And notice the language of unfaithfulness: whoring heart, eyes that go whoring. Idolatry is adultery. It begins in the heart and the eyes before it ever reaches a hilltop altar.

Then the fruit of remembering: they will be loathsome in their own sight. When the exiles finally see what their sin did to God, they will hate it. Ezekiel will say this again: you will remember your evil ways... and you will loathe yourselves (36:31). That is not self-hatred for its own sake. It is the beginning of true repentance — seeing sin from God's side. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret (2 Cor 7:10).

And they shall know that I am the LORD. I have not said in vain that I would do this evil to them."

Not... in vain. God's warnings were not empty threats. The people had heard them for so long that they had stopped believing them. God keeps his word — in warning and in promise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel is to clap his hands, stamp his foot and cry Alas over Israel's abominations (v. 11). Pestilence, sword and famine will reach the far and the near (v. 12). Their slain will lie among their idols on every high hill and under every green tree (v. 13), and the land will be desolate from the wilderness to Riblah (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Where people worshipped their idols, there their ruin will be seen.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: "Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Alas, because of all the evil abominations of the house of Israel, for they shall fall by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence. He who is far off shall die of pestilence, and he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who is left and is preserved shall die of famine. Thus I will spend my fury upon them. And you shall know that I am the LORD, when their slain lie among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the mountaintops, under every green tree, and under every leafy oak, wherever they offered pleasing aroma to all their idols. And I will stretch out my hand against them and make the land desolate and waste, in all their dwelling places, from the wilderness to Riblah. Then they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the Lord GOD: "Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Alas, because of all the evil abominations of the house of Israel, for they shall fall by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence.

Ezekiel must act out his grief: clap, stamp, cry Alas. The message is not delivered calmly from a distance. The prophet feels it in his body.

Anyone who speaks about God's judgment should speak like this — not with satisfaction, but with anguish.

He who is far off shall die of pestilence, and he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who is left and is preserved shall die of famine. Thus I will spend my fury upon them.

Far or near, fleeing or staying, there is no hiding place. Those who run die of disease; those close by die by the sword; those who hold out inside die of hunger.

And you shall know that I am the LORD, when their slain lie among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the mountaintops, under every green tree, and under every leafy oak, wherever they offered pleasing aroma to all their idols.

Pleasing aroma was the language of sacrifices God accepted. Israel offered it to idols instead. So the places of their false worship become the places of their death.

And I will stretch out my hand against them and make the land desolate and waste, in all their dwelling places, from the wilderness to Riblah. Then they will know that I am the LORD."

From the southern wilderness to the far north — the whole land. (The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read "Diblah".) If Riblah is the right reading, it would become a name of horror: it was there that Zedekiah watched his sons killed before his eyes were put out (Jer 39:6-7).

The same hand that once stretched out to bring Israel out of Egypt is stretched out against them. But the book will not end there. The God who says I will stretch out my hand in judgment is also the God who says, a few chapters on, I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them (11:19).

6.title: Against the Mountains of Israel
6.overview:
Ezekiel is told to set his face toward the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them. God will bring a sword on the hills, ravines and valleys, destroy the high places, break the altars, and lay the dead bodies of his people before their idols with their bones scattered around the altars. Every city will be waste and every idol broken, and they will know that he is the LORD (vv. 1-7).

Yet God will leave some alive. Among the nations the survivors will remember him, and how he was broken over their unfaithful hearts and eyes that went after idols; they will loathe themselves for their evils and know that God did not speak in vain (vv. 8-10).

Ezekiel is to clap his hands, stamp his foot and cry Alas. Pestilence, sword and famine will reach far and near. Their slain will lie among their idols on every high hill and under every green tree, and God will make the land desolate from the wilderness to Riblah, and they will know that he is the LORD (vv. 11-14).
6.theology:
God's word reaches wherever he sends it, even to distant mountains (vv. 1-3).

Idols cannot save; their worshippers will lie dead before them (vv. 4-6; Ps 115:4-8).

Judgment is not God's final word: he leaves a remnant (v. 8).

Idolatry is spiritual adultery that begins in the heart and eyes, and it breaks God's heart (v. 9; Gen 6:6; Matt 23:37; Eph 4:30).

True repentance sees sin from God's side and loathes it (v. 9; 36:31; 2 Cor 7:10).

God's warnings are not in vain; he does what he says (v. 10).
6.examples:
A prophet in Babylon preaching to the hills of home.

Worshippers lying dead in front of gods that cannot see them.

A God who says: I have been broken.

Eyes that go whoring before the feet ever climb the hill.

Clapping, stamping and crying Alas.

The end has come upon the four corners of the land.<sup>3</sup>Now the end is upon you, and I will send my anger upon you; I will judge you according to your ways, and I will punish you for all your abominations.<sup>4</sup>And my eye will not spare you, nor will I have pity, but I will punish you for your ways, while your abominations are in your midst. He who is in the field dies by the sword, and him who is in the city famine and pestilence devour.<sup>16</sup>And if any survivors escape, they will be on the mountains, like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, each one over his iniquity.<sup>17</sup>All hands are feeble, and all knees turn to water.<sup>18</sup>They put on sackcloth, and horror covers them. Shame is on all faces, and baldness on all their heads.<sup>19</sup>They cast their silver into the streets, and their gold is like an unclean thing. Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD. They cannot satisfy their hunger or fill their stomachs with it. For it was the stumbling block of their iniquity.<sup>20</sup>His beautiful ornament they used for pride, and they made their abominable images and their detestable things of it. Therefore I make it an unclean thing to them.<sup>21</sup>And I will give it into the hands of foreigners for prey, and to the wicked of the earth for spoil, and they shall profane it.<sup>22</sup>I will turn my face from them, and they shall profane my treasured place. Robbers shall enter and profane it.<sup>23</sup>"Forge a chain! For the land is full of bloody crimes and the city is full of violence.<sup>24</sup>I will bring the worst of the nations to take possession of their houses. I will put an end to the pride of the strong, and their holy places shall be profaned.<sup>25</sup>When anguish comes, they will seek peace, but there shall be none.<sup>26</sup>Disaster comes upon disaster; rumor follows rumor. According to their way I will do to them, and according to their judgments I will judge them, and they shall know that I am the LORD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — An End! The End Has Come
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land (v. 2). God will send his anger and judge Judah according to its ways (vv. 3-4). Disaster after disaster! Behold, it comes (v. 5); the end has awakened, the day is near, a day of tumult (vv. 6-7). God will pour out his wrath without pity, Then you will know that I am the LORD, who strikes (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: There is a real end to God's patience, and it comes on the day he has set.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "And you, O son of man, thus says the Lord GOD to the land of Israel: An end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land. Now the end is upon you, and I will send my anger upon you; I will judge you according to your ways, and I will punish you for all your abominations. And my eye will not spare you, nor will I have pity, but I will punish you for your ways, while your abominations are in your midst. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to me:

"And you, O son of man, thus says the Lord GOD to the land of Israel: An end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land.

Chapter 7 reads like a bell tolling. An end! The end has come. The word end strikes again and again in the opening verses. For centuries Israel had heard warnings. Now the warnings are over.

More than a century and a half earlier the LORD had said the same thing to the northern kingdom through Amos: The end has come upon my people Israel (Amos 8:2). The north did not listen, and it fell. Now Judah hears the same sentence.

The four corners of the land — the whole of it, nowhere excluded. The ESV notes that land may be "earth", as if Judah's end were a picture of a greater end still to come for all the world.

Now the end is upon you, and I will send my anger upon you; I will judge you according to your ways, and I will punish you for all your abominations.

According to your ways. Judgment is not random. It fits what was done. God does not punish people for sins they did not commit, and he does not overlook the ones they did.

And my eye will not spare you, nor will I have pity, but I will punish you for your ways, while your abominations are in your midst. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

While your abominations are in your midst. They are still clinging to their idols even as the end comes. God's patience has been long, but it has not been answered with repentance. Do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience? (Rom 2:4).

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: Disaster after disaster! Behold, it comes. An end has come; the end has come; it has awakened against you. Behold, it comes. Your doom has come to you, O inhabitant of the land. The time has come; the day is near, a day of tumult, and not of joyful shouting on the mountains. Now I will soon pour out my wrath upon you, and spend my anger against you, and judge you according to your ways, and I will punish you for all your abominations. And my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity. I will punish you according to your ways, while your abominations are in your midst. Then you will know that I am the LORD, who strikes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the Lord GOD: Disaster after disaster! Behold, it comes.

The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read "Disaster! A unique disaster!" Either one disaster after another, or one disaster like no other.

An end has come; the end has come; it has awakened against you. Behold, it comes.

The end has awakened. For years people said the judgment was asleep, that nothing would happen. Peter describes the same attitude in the last days: scoffers asking Where is the promise of his coming? (2 Pet 3:4). But The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, and the day of the Lord will come like a thief (2 Pet 3:9-10). What looks like sleep is patience.

Your doom has come to you, O inhabitant of the land. The time has come; the day is near, a day of tumult, and not of joyful shouting on the mountains.

The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew word behind doom is uncertain. But the picture is clear: the mountains, where people shouted at harvest festivals and at idol feasts, will hear a different noise — the tumult of an invading army.

Now I will soon pour out my wrath upon you, and spend my anger against you, and judge you according to your ways, and I will punish you for all your abominations.

And my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity. I will punish you according to your ways, while your abominations are in your midst. Then you will know that I am the LORD, who strikes.

Verses 8-9 repeat verses 3-4 almost word for word. The repetition hammers the message home. And a new name is added at the end: the LORD, who strikes. They had known him as the LORD who delivers, who provides, who blesses. They had forgotten that he also strikes. A God who never judges is not the God of the Bible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–22 — Silver and Gold Cannot Deliver
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rod has blossomed and pride has budded (v. 10); violence has grown into wickedness, and nothing of their wealth will remain (v. 11). Buying and selling lose their meaning (vv. 12-13). The trumpet sounds but no one goes to battle; sword outside, famine and pestilence inside (vv. 14-15). Survivors moan on the mountains, hands limp, knees like water, faces covered with shame (vv. 16-18). They throw their silver into the streets, because Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD (v. 19). The jewellery they made into idols will be given to foreigners, and robbers will profane God's treasured place (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The wealth people trust becomes worthless on the day of God's wrath, and the thing they made into an idol becomes their stumbling block.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the day! Behold, it comes! Your doom has come; the rod has blossomed; pride has budded. Violence has grown up into a rod of wickedness. None of them shall remain, nor their abundance, nor their wealth; neither shall there be preeminence among them. The time has come; the day has arrived. Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn, for wrath is upon all their multitude. For the seller shall not return to what he has sold, while they live. For the vision concerns all their multitude; it shall not turn back; and because of his iniquity, none can maintain his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the day! Behold, it comes! Your doom has come; the rod has blossomed; pride has budded.

The rod has blossomed; pride has budded. Like a plant that has been growing quietly, Judah's pride has come into flower — and so has the rod of punishment. Perhaps there is an echo of Aaron's staff, which had sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms as a sign of God's choosing (Num 17:8); if so, what once blossomed as a sign of God's favour now blossoms as a sign of his judgment. Sin has a growing season, and then it flowers.

Violence has grown up into a rod of wickedness. None of them shall remain, nor their abundance, nor their wealth; neither shall there be preeminence among them.

The ESV notes that the meaning of the last sentence is uncertain, but the thrust is plain. The violence Judah practised has grown into the rod that will beat it. None of their wealth, none of their rank, will survive.

The time has come; the day has arrived. Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn, for wrath is upon all their multitude.

Normally the buyer is glad of a good deal and the seller sorry to part with land. But when the end comes, neither matters. The buyer will not keep what he bought; the seller has lost nothing worth grieving. (The ESV notes that multitude may be "abundance".)

For the seller shall not return to what he has sold, while they live. For the vision concerns all their multitude; it shall not turn back; and because of his iniquity, none can maintain his life.

Under the law, land sold returned to its family in the year of jubilee (Lev 25:13). That hope is gone: the seller shall not return. Exile will outlast them.

Paul applies the same perspective to Christians: let... those who buy live as though they had no goods... For the present form of this world is passing away (1 Cor 7:30-31). The end of all things puts property in its place. Hold what you own loosely.

verseByVerse.quote: "They have blown the trumpet and made everything ready, but none goes to battle, for my wrath is upon all their multitude. The sword is without; pestilence and famine are within. He who is in the field dies by the sword, and him who is in the city famine and pestilence devour. And if any survivors escape, they will be on the mountains, like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, each one over his iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They have blown the trumpet and made everything ready, but none goes to battle, for my wrath is upon all their multitude.

The trumpet sounds. The weapons are ready. And no one marches out. Courage has simply drained away, because God's wrath is on them. An army without God's blessing is paralysed.

The sword is without; pestilence and famine are within. He who is in the field dies by the sword, and him who is in the city famine and pestilence devour.

Field or city, there is nowhere safe. Stay out in the country and the sword finds you; shelter behind the walls and hunger and disease find you. Amos pictured the same inescapable day: as if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him, or went into the house and leaned his hand against the wall, and a serpent bit him (Amos 5:19). There is no hiding place from God except in God himself.

And if any survivors escape, they will be on the mountains, like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, each one over his iniquity.

The few who get away hide in the hills, moaning like mourning doves. And at last they are moaning over the right thing: each one over his iniquity. Suffering has finally driven them to face their sin. It is a terrible way to come to repentance, but it is better than never coming at all.

verseByVerse.quote: All hands are feeble, and all knees turn to water. They put on sackcloth, and horror covers them. Shame is on all faces, and baldness on all their heads. They cast their silver into the streets, and their gold is like an unclean thing. Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD. They cannot satisfy their hunger or fill their stomachs with it. For it was the stumbling block of their iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All hands are feeble, and all knees turn to water.

They put on sackcloth, and horror covers them. Shame is on all faces, and baldness on all their heads.

Limp hands, knees that give way, sackcloth, shaved heads, faces burning with shame. The proud city of verse 10 is reduced to mourners. Pride always ends in shame when God acts.

They cast their silver into the streets, and their gold is like an unclean thing. Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD. They cannot satisfy their hunger or fill their stomachs with it. For it was the stumbling block of their iniquity.

Imagine people throwing silver into the gutter because it is useless. You cannot eat gold in a siege. You cannot buy your way out of God's judgment. Zephaniah said it in almost the same words: Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the LORD (Zeph 1:18). Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death (Prov 11:4).

And more than useless — it was the stumbling block of their iniquity. Their wealth was what tripped them up. Money had fed their pride, paid for their idols and bought their comfort while the poor suffered.

This is a searching word in a wealthy culture. What we trust for security may be exactly what keeps us from God. What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? (Matt 16:26). There is only one ransom that works on the day of wrath, and it was not paid with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19).

verseByVerse.quote: His beautiful ornament they used for pride, and they made their abominable images and their detestable things of it. Therefore I make it an unclean thing to them. And I will give it into the hands of foreigners for prey, and to the wicked of the earth for spoil, and they shall profane it. I will turn my face from them, and they shall profane my treasured place. Robbers shall enter and profane it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His beautiful ornament they used for pride, and they made their abominable images and their detestable things of it. Therefore I make it an unclean thing to them.

The gold God had given them as a beautiful ornament they turned into a source of pride and then melted down into idols. It is the golden calf all over again: the people took the rings of gold that were in their ears, and Aaron made a golden calf (Exod 32:3-4). God's gifts, turned against the Giver.

And I will give it into the hands of foreigners for prey, and to the wicked of the earth for spoil, and they shall profane it.

I will turn my face from them, and they shall profane my treasured place. Robbers shall enter and profane it.

My treasured place — the ESV notes it may be "secret" place — is the temple, and most of all its inner sanctuary. Robbers will walk into it. And the reason is given first: I will turn my face from them. The temple's protection was never its walls. It was God's face turned toward his people. When he turns away, anyone can walk in.

And look who God uses: foreigners, the wicked of the earth. That troubled the prophet Habakkuk deeply, when God told him I am raising up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation. He asked how a holy God could remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he (Hab 1:6, 13). The answer Scripture gives is that God can use wicked instruments to accomplish just purposes, and then hold those instruments accountable for their own wickedness — as he did with Babylon.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Forge a chain! For the land is full of bloody crimes and the city is full of violence (v. 23). The worst of the nations will take their houses (v. 24). They will seek peace and find none (v. 25); they will seek a vision from the prophet, but the law will perish from the priest and counsel from the elders (v. 26). King, prince and people will be paralysed, and God will judge them by their own standards, and they shall know that I am the LORD (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: When the end comes, every source of guidance people once ignored is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: "Forge a chain! For the land is full of bloody crimes and the city is full of violence. I will bring the worst of the nations to take possession of their houses. I will put an end to the pride of the strong, and their holy places shall be profaned. When anguish comes, they will seek peace, but there shall be none.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Forge a chain! For the land is full of bloody crimes and the city is full of violence.

The ESV notes that the chain probably refers to an instrument of captivity. Make the chains ready; the captives are coming. And the reason again is not idolatry alone but bloody crimes and violence. Sin against God always shows itself as sin against neighbour.

I will bring the worst of the nations to take possession of their houses. I will put an end to the pride of the strong, and their holy places shall be profaned.

The worst of the nations — ruthless Babylon — will move into Judah's homes. (Where the ESV reads their holy places, it notes the Hebrew as "those who sanctify them".)

I will put an end to the pride of the strong. Judah's leaders had trusted their strength, their alliances and their fortress city. God's way through history is always the same: he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate (Luke 1:52). The strong who will not bow will be humbled.

When anguish comes, they will seek peace, but there shall be none.

For years the false prophets had promised peace: saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace (Jer 6:14). Now the people seek it and find nothing. There is a time when peace with God can be found, and a time when it is too late. Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Disaster comes upon disaster; rumor follows rumor. They seek a vision from the prophet, while the law perishes from the priest and counsel from the elders. The king mourns, the prince is wrapped in despair, and the hands of the people of the land are paralyzed by terror. According to their way I will do to them, and according to their judgments I will judge them, and they shall know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Disaster comes upon disaster; rumor follows rumor. They seek a vision from the prophet, while the law perishes from the priest and counsel from the elders.

Now, too late, they want to hear from God. They run to the prophet for a vision. But the priest has no instruction (the ESV notes law may be "instruction") and the elders have no counsel. The very sources of guidance they had ignored for years are gone. Lamentations mourned it: the law is no more, and her prophets find no vision from the LORD (Lam 2:9).

Do not assume God's word will always be available when you finally want it.

The king mourns, the prince is wrapped in despair, and the hands of the people of the land are paralyzed by terror. According to their way I will do to them, and according to their judgments I will judge them, and they shall know that I am the LORD."

From the king down to the ordinary people, everyone is paralysed. And the last sentence is exact justice: according to their judgments I will judge them. They were harsh and unjust to others; God will measure them with their own measure. Jesus warned, with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged (Matt 7:2).

And yet, for those in Christ, the end has already come in another sense. Christ has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Heb 9:26). The end fell on him. Those who are joined to him do not face the end as doom; they are the ones on whom the end of the ages has come (1 Cor 10:11) as salvation.

7.title: The End Has Come
7.overview:
God announces an end: the end has come on the four corners of the land. He will send his anger and judge Judah according to its ways, without pity, while their abominations are still in their midst. Disaster after disaster is coming; the end has awakened and the day of tumult is near. God will pour out his wrath, and they will know that he is the LORD who strikes (vv. 1-9).

The rod has blossomed and pride has budded; violence has grown into wickedness, and none of their wealth or rank will remain. Buying and selling no longer matter. The trumpet sounds but no one goes to battle; sword is outside and famine and pestilence inside. Survivors moan on the mountains over their iniquity, weak with fear and covered with shame. They throw their silver into the streets, because silver and gold cannot deliver them in the day of the LORD's wrath; it was the stumbling block of their iniquity. The ornaments they made into idols will be given to foreigners, and robbers will profane God's treasured place (vv. 10-22).

Chains are to be made, for the land is full of bloodshed and violence. The worst of the nations will take their houses. They will seek peace and find none, seek a vision from the prophet while the law perishes from the priest and counsel from the elders. King, prince and people will be paralysed, and God will judge them by their own judgments, and they will know that he is the LORD (vv. 23-27).
7.theology:
God's patience has an end, and judgment fits the ways of those judged (vv. 2-4, 27; Amos 8:2; Rom 2:4-5).

The LORD who delivers is also the LORD who strikes (v. 9).

Wealth cannot deliver in the day of wrath and often becomes the very stumbling block of sin (v. 19; Zeph 1:18; Prov 11:4; Matt 16:26).

God's gifts turned into idols become unclean to their owners (vv. 20-22; Exod 32:2-4).

The protection of God's house is God's face, not its walls (v. 22).

Guidance ignored may be withdrawn when it is finally sought (vv. 25-26; Lam 2:9).

The end of the ages fell on Christ, so that for those in him the end is salvation, not doom (Heb 9:26; 1 Cor 10:11).
7.examples:
A bell tolling: the end, the end, the end.

Pride coming into flower.

A buyer and seller who both lose.

A trumpet blast and nobody marching.

Silver thrown into the gutter.

Jewellery melted into idols.

Running to the prophet when there are no more visions.

Below what appeared to be his waist was fire, and above his waist was something like the appearance of brightness, like gleaming metal.<sup>3</sup>He put out the form of a hand and took me by a lock of my head, and the Spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven and brought me in visions of God to Jerusalem, to the entrance of the gateway of the inner court that faces north, where was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy.<sup>4</sup>And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, like the vision that I saw in the valley.<sup>5</sup>Then he said to me, "Son of man, lift up your eyes now toward the north."
