verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Fourteen months after his call, with the elders of Judah sitting before him, Ezekiel is seized by the hand of the Lord GOD (v. 1). A fiery figure lifts him by his hair and carries him in visions of God to Jerusalem, to the north gate of the inner court, where stands the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy (vv. 2-3). The glory of God is there too (v. 4). The image stands right at the altar gate (v. 5), and God asks whether Ezekiel sees what they are doing to drive me far from my sanctuary (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry in God's house provokes his jealousy and drives his presence away.

verseByVerse.quote: In the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I sat in my house, with the elders of Judah sitting before me, the hand of the Lord GOD fell upon me there. Then I looked, and behold, a form that had the appearance of a man. Below what appeared to be his waist was fire, and above his waist was something like the appearance of brightness, like gleaming metal. He put out the form of a hand and took me by a lock of my head, and the Spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven and brought me in visions of God to Jerusalem, to the entrance of the gateway of the inner court that faces north, where was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I sat in my house, with the elders of Judah sitting before me, the hand of the Lord GOD fell upon me there.

About fourteen months have passed since the first vision. The leaders of the exiles have come to Ezekiel's house and sit before him, presumably to hear a word from God. They get more than they expected. The vision that follows is God's answer to every exile who thought Jerusalem was innocent and would be spared.

Then I looked, and behold, a form that had the appearance of a man. Below what appeared to be his waist was fire, and above his waist was something like the appearance of brightness, like gleaming metal.

This is the same figure Ezekiel saw on the throne (1:27): fire below, brightness above. (The ESV follows the Septuagint for a man; the Hebrew reads "fire", and it notes that gleaming metal may be "amber".) The one who will show him the temple is the Lord himself.

He put out the form of a hand and took me by a lock of my head, and the Spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven and brought me in visions of God to Jerusalem, to the entrance of the gateway of the inner court that faces north, where was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy.

Ezekiel does not travel in body; he is taken in visions of God. But what he sees is real. He is set down at the gate of the inner court, and the first thing in front of him is an idol: the image of jealousy.

God had said at Sinai, You shall not make for yourself a carved image... for I the LORD your God am a jealous God (Exod 20:4-5). An idol in his house is like a lover's photograph on a married couple's bedside table. They stirred him to jealousy with strange gods (Deut 32:16). King Manasseh had once set the carved image of Asherah inside the temple (2 Kgs 21:7). The reforms since then had not lasted.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, like the vision that I saw in the valley. Then he said to me, "Son of man, lift up your eyes now toward the north." So I lifted up my eyes toward the north, and behold, north of the altar gate, in the entrance, was this image of jealousy. And he said to me, "Son of man, do you see what they are doing, the great abominations that the house of Israel are committing here, to drive me far from my sanctuary? But you will see still greater abominations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, like the vision that I saw in the valley.

Both are in the courtyard at once: the glory of God and the image of jealousy. That is the tension of the whole vision. How long can the holy God stay in a house where an idol stands at the gate?

Then he said to me, "Son of man, lift up your eyes now toward the north." So I lifted up my eyes toward the north, and behold, north of the altar gate, in the entrance, was this image of jealousy.

North of the altar gate. The idol stands by the way to the altar, where sacrifices for sin were offered. People passing to worship the LORD walked past it. Religion had become a mixture.

And he said to me, "Son of man, do you see what they are doing, the great abominations that the house of Israel are committing here, to drive me far from my sanctuary? But you will see still greater abominations."

Here is the reason the glory will leave in chapters 10-11. God does not simply abandon his house. His people drive him out. Sin pushes God away.

That applies to Christians too. Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you? (1 Cor 3:16). The Spirit does not leave a true believer. But believers can grieve him and lose the felt sense of his nearness when they make room for idols in the heart.

And the refrain begins: you will see still greater abominations. Each room Ezekiel enters is worse than the last.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Through a hole in the wall Ezekiel digs into a hidden room (vv. 7-9) whose walls are carved with creeping things, unclean beasts and idols (v. 10). Seventy elders of Israel stand before them with censers of incense, Jaazaniah son of Shaphan among them (v. 11), saying The LORD does not see us, the LORD has forsaken the land (v. 12). And there is worse to see (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Secret sin is never hidden from God, and it is often most at home among the leaders.

verseByVerse.quote: And he brought me to the entrance of the court, and when I looked, behold, there was a hole in the wall. Then he said to me, "Son of man, dig in the wall." So I dug in the wall, and behold, there was an entrance. And he said to me, "Go in, and see the vile abominations that they are committing here." So I went in and saw. And there, engraved on the wall all around, was every form of creeping things and loathsome beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he brought me to the entrance of the court, and when I looked, behold, there was a hole in the wall.

Then he said to me, "Son of man, dig in the wall." So I dug in the wall, and behold, there was an entrance.

And he said to me, "Go in, and see the vile abominations that they are committing here."

Picture it: a hole, then digging, then a hidden doorway. This worship happens out of sight, behind walls, in a secret room. It is the religion of people who know what they are doing is wrong.

So I went in and saw. And there, engraved on the wall all around, was every form of creeping things and loathsome beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel.

The walls are covered with carvings of reptiles, insects and unclean animals — exactly what the law forbade: the likeness of any animal that is on the earth... the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground (Deut 4:17-18). Paul describes the same exchange in every culture: people exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things (Rom 1:23).

The glory of God is in the court. In the dark room they bow to beetles and snakes. That is the tragic foolishness of all idolatry — trading the Creator for creeping things.

verseByVerse.quote: And before them stood seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, with Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan standing among them. Each had his censer in his hand, and the smoke of the cloud of incense went up. Then he said to me, "Son of man, have you seen what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the dark, each in his room of pictures? For they say, 'The LORD does not see us, the LORD has forsaken the land.'" He said also to me, "You will see still greater abominations that they commit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And before them stood seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, with Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan standing among them. Each had his censer in his hand, and the smoke of the cloud of incense went up.

Seventy men of the elders. The number is deliberate. At Sinai, seventy of the elders of Israel went up the mountain, and they saw the God of Israel (Exod 24:9-10). Their successors now burn incense to carved animals in a dark room.

And one man is named: Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan. If this is the Shaphan who served King Josiah during the great reform (2 Kgs 22:12), whose son Ahikam protected Jeremiah (Jer 26:24), then this is a son of a faithful family. Godly parents do not guarantee godly children. Every generation must turn to God for itself.

Then he said to me, "Son of man, have you seen what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the dark, each in his room of pictures? For they say, 'The LORD does not see us, the LORD has forsaken the land.'"

Each in his room of pictures. Not only one room: each had his own private shrine. And their excuse is theology: The LORD does not see us, the LORD has forsaken the land. Since the exile of Jehoiachin, God seemed absent, so they looked for other help.

But Ezekiel has seen the wheels full of eyes all around (1:18). He who formed the eye, does he not see? (Ps 94:9). No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Heb 4:13).

Many people today have a room of pictures — a hidden screen, a secret habit, a private idol — kept behind a wall while they carry the censer in public. God sees into that room. And he sees it so that it can be brought into the light and forgiven, before it is exposed in judgment.

He said also to me, "You will see still greater abominations that they commit."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the north gate women sit weeping for Tammuz (vv. 14-15). In the inner court, between the porch and the altar, about twenty-five men stand with their backs to the temple of the LORD, bowing to the sun in the east (v. 16). They fill the land with violence and provoke God still further (v. 17), so he will act in wrath, And though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: To turn your back on God while standing in his house is the height of rebellion, and it invites his judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me to the entrance of the north gate of the house of the LORD, and behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz. Then he said to me, "Have you seen this, O son of man? You will see still greater abominations than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he brought me to the entrance of the north gate of the house of the LORD, and behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz.

Tammuz was a god whose death was ritually mourned in the ancient Near East, tied to the dying of vegetation in the dry season. Women sit at the gate of the LORD's house weeping for a dead god.

The irony is sharp. They have the living God, and they weep for a god who cannot rise. They are grieving over the wrong death. The death to weep over and to trust in is the death of the one who rose again.

Then he said to me, "Have you seen this, O son of man? You will see still greater abominations than these."

verseByVerse.quote: And he brought me into the inner court of the house of the LORD. And behold, at the entrance of the temple of the LORD, between the porch and the altar, were about twenty-five men, with their backs to the temple of the LORD, and their faces toward the east, worshiping the sun toward the east. Then he said to me, "Have you seen this, O son of man? Is it too light a thing for the house of Judah to commit the abominations that they commit here, that they should fill the land with violence and provoke me still further to anger? Behold, they put the branch to their nose. Therefore I will act in wrath. My eye will not spare, nor will I have pity. And though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he brought me into the inner court of the house of the LORD. And behold, at the entrance of the temple of the LORD, between the porch and the altar, were about twenty-five men, with their backs to the temple of the LORD, and their faces toward the east, worshiping the sun toward the east.

Now the innermost court, between the porch and the altar — the place where the priests stood to pray for the people. About twenty-five men stand there with their backs to God's house and bow to the rising sun.

Moses had warned, beware lest you raise your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars... you be drawn away and bow down to them (Deut 4:19). Josiah had removed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun, at the entrance to the house of the LORD (2 Kgs 23:11). Now it is back, at the very centre.

The posture says everything. Backs to the temple of the LORD. God had said through Jeremiah, they have turned their back to me, and not their face (Jer 2:27). You can stand in the right building and have your back to God.

Then he said to me, "Have you seen this, O son of man? Is it too light a thing for the house of Judah to commit the abominations that they commit here, that they should fill the land with violence and provoke me still further to anger? Behold, they put the branch to their nose.

False worship and violence go together. When people turn their back on God, they soon turn their fists on each other.

They put the branch to their nose is an obscure gesture, and no one is sure what it meant. The ESV notes that their may be "my" — which would make it an insult pushed into God's own face.

Therefore I will act in wrath. My eye will not spare, nor will I have pity. And though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them."

The final words are terrible: though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them. Wisdom had warned long ago: they will call upon me, but I will not answer (Prov 1:28). There is a time when calling on God is too late.

But notice where this vision is being told: to elders sitting in a house in Babylon, while there is still time. The warning is itself mercy. Jesus, finding his Father's house full of traders, drove them out, and His disciples remembered that it was written, "Zeal for your house will consume me" (John 2:17). His zeal did consume him: he died so that a people could become a temple where God is worshipped in spirit and truth (John 4:23).

8.title: Abominations in the Temple
8.overview:
In the sixth year, as the elders of Judah sit before him, Ezekiel sees again the fiery figure of the glory, who takes him by the hair and brings him in visions of God to Jerusalem. At the north gate of the inner court stands the image of jealousy, and the glory of God is there too. God shows him the abominations that are driving him from his sanctuary and promises greater ones (vv. 1-6).

Through a hole in the wall Ezekiel digs into a secret room whose walls are carved with creeping things, unclean animals and idols. Seventy elders of Israel, Jaazaniah son of Shaphan among them, offer incense there in the dark, saying the LORD does not see them and has forsaken the land (vv. 7-13).

At the north gate women weep for Tammuz. In the inner court, between the porch and the altar, about twenty-five men stand with their backs to the temple and worship the sun. They fill the land with violence and provoke God further, so he will act in wrath without pity, and will not hear them even when they cry aloud (vv. 14-18).
8.theology:
God is jealous for his people's exclusive worship, and idolatry in his house drives his presence away (vv. 3, 5-6; Exod 20:4-5; Deut 32:16).

Idolatry exchanges the glory of God for images of creatures (v. 10; Deut 4:16-18; Rom 1:22-23).

Secret sin is seen by God; the claim that he does not see is folly (v. 12; Ps 94:7-9; Heb 4:13).

Leaders bear special guilt when they lead God's people into false worship (vv. 11, 16).

False worship and social violence belong together (v. 17).

There comes a time when cries for help are too late (v. 18; Prov 1:28); the warning given beforehand is mercy.

Christ's zeal for his Father's house led him to the cross, to make a people who worship in spirit and truth and are themselves God's temple (John 2:17; 4:23-24; 1 Cor 3:16-17).
8.examples:
An idol standing by the gate to the altar.

Digging through a wall into a room of pictures.

Seventy elders burning incense to beetles.

A son of a faithful family holding a censer in the dark.

Weeping for a god who stays dead.

Standing in God's house with your back to him.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Then he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying, "Bring near the executioners of the city, each with his destroying weapon in his hand."<sup>2</sup>And behold, six men came from the direction of the upper gate, which faces north, each with his weapon for slaughter in his hand, and with them was a man clothed in linen, with a writing case at his waist. And they went in and stood beside the bronze altar.<sup>3</sup>Now the glory of the God of Israel had gone up from the cherub on which it rested to the threshold of the house. And he called to the man clothed in linen, who had the writing case at his waist.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to him, "Pass through the city, through Jerusalem, and put a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it."<sup>5</sup>And to the others he said in my hearing, "Pass through the city after him, and strike. Your eye shall not spare, and you shall show no pity.<sup>6</sup>Kill old men outright, young men and maidens, little children and women, but touch no one on whom is the mark. And begin at my sanctuary." So they began with the elders who were before the house.<sup>7</sup>Then he said to them, "Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain. Go out." So they went out and struck in the city.<sup>8</sup>And while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, "Ah, Lord GOD! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel in the outpouring of your wrath on Jerusalem?"<sup>9</sup>Then he said to me, "The guilt of the house of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. The land is full of blood, and the city full of injustice. For they say, 'The LORD has forsaken the land, and the LORD does not see.'<sup>10</sup>As for me, my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity; I will bring their deeds upon their heads."<sup>11</sup>And behold, the man clothed in linen, with the writing case at his waist, brought back word, saying, "I have done as you commanded me."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — A Man Clothed in Linen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls for the executioners of the city: six men with weapons, and among them a man clothed in linen with a writing case (vv. 1-2). The glory rises from the cherub to the threshold of the temple (v. 3), and the man in linen is sent through Jerusalem to put a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Before judgment falls, God marks and protects those who grieve over sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying, "Bring near the executioners of the city, each with his destroying weapon in his hand." And behold, six men came from the direction of the upper gate, which faces north, each with his weapon for slaughter in his hand, and with them was a man clothed in linen, with a writing case at his waist. And they went in and stood beside the bronze altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying, "Bring near the executioners of the city, each with his destroying weapon in his hand."

The last verse of chapter 8 said the people would cry in my ears with a loud voice and God would not hear. Now God cries in my ears with a loud voice — calling for the executioners. The people's cry comes too late; God's cry comes on time.

And behold, six men came from the direction of the upper gate, which faces north, each with his weapon for slaughter in his hand, and with them was a man clothed in linen, with a writing case at his waist. And they went in and stood beside the bronze altar.

This is a vision, so these are heavenly agents of judgment, though on earth God would use Babylon's army. Six carry weapons. The seventh is different: he wears linen, the fabric of priests (Lev 16:4), and carries a scribe's writing case instead of a sword. Daniel saw a man clothed in linen too (Dan 10:5).

They take their stand beside the bronze altar — the altar of sacrifice. Judgment starts where atonement was supposed to happen. The people had kept the sacrifices going and ignored the God they were offered to.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the glory of the God of Israel had gone up from the cherub on which it rested to the threshold of the house. And he called to the man clothed in linen, who had the writing case at his waist. And the LORD said to him, "Pass through the city, through Jerusalem, and put a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the glory of the God of Israel had gone up from the cherub on which it rested to the threshold of the house. And he called to the man clothed in linen, who had the writing case at his waist.

Watch the glory. It has moved from its place above the cherubim in the Most Holy Place to the threshold of the house, the doorway. The departure has begun. God leaves his house step by step, slowly, as if reluctant to go.

And the LORD said to him, "Pass through the city, through Jerusalem, and put a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it."

Before anyone is struck, God protects his own. The man in linen goes first and marks every person who sigh and groan over all the abominations.

It is the Passover again: The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you (Exod 12:13). And it looks forward to the last judgment, when God's servants are sealed... on their foreheads and the plagues harm only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads (Rev 7:3; 9:4). The Lord knows those who are his (2 Tim 2:19).

Who receives the mark? Not the people who performed the right rituals, but those who sigh and groan over sin. The psalmist was one of them: My eyes shed streams of tears, because people do not keep your law (Ps 119:136).

Here is a probing question for every believer. When you see sin in the church and in the culture — and in your own heart — do you shrug, or sneer, or grieve? The people God marks are the grieving ones.

And for Christians, the one who marks us is Christ, the true priest, and the mark is his Spirit: when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Eph 1:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The others are told to strike without pity, sparing only those with the mark, And begin at my sanctuary — so they begin with the elders before the temple (vv. 5-7). Ezekiel falls on his face and cries, Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel? (v. 8). God answers that the guilt is exceedingly great, the land full of blood and injustice, and the people say he does not see (vv. 9-10). The man in linen returns: I have done as you commanded me (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment begins with those closest to God's house, and God's servants plead for mercy even as it falls.

verseByVerse.quote: And to the others he said in my hearing, "Pass through the city after him, and strike. Your eye shall not spare, and you shall show no pity. Kill old men outright, young men and maidens, little children and women, but touch no one on whom is the mark. And begin at my sanctuary." So they began with the elders who were before the house. Then he said to them, "Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain. Go out." So they went out and struck in the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And to the others he said in my hearing, "Pass through the city after him, and strike. Your eye shall not spare, and you shall show no pity.

Kill old men outright, young men and maidens, little children and women, but touch no one on whom is the mark. And begin at my sanctuary." So they began with the elders who were before the house.

These are hard words, and they should not be softened. When Jerusalem fell, all ages suffered. Children die when cities are destroyed. The Bible does not pretend otherwise.

What do we do with this? First, remember whose judgment it is. Abraham, pleading for Sodom, held on to one certainty: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Gen 18:25). We do not see as God sees, and we do not know every heart. Second, notice the exception, stated in the same breath: touch no one on whom is the mark. God's judgment is not indiscriminate; he knows his own. Third, this is a vision of what sin brings on a whole community, and it is meant to terrify people into repentance while there is time.

Begin at my sanctuary. Judgment starts with the people nearest to God's house, and with its leaders — the elders who were before the house, perhaps the very men Ezekiel had seen with their backs to the temple (8:16). Peter says the same principle holds for the church: it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God (1 Pet 4:17). Privilege brings accountability.

Then he said to them, "Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain. Go out." So they went out and struck in the city.

Defile the house. God himself commands the defiling of his temple. The people had already defiled it with idols; now corpses will make that defilement visible. A holy God will not protect a building that has become a shrine to other gods.

verseByVerse.quote: And while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, "Ah, Lord GOD! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel in the outpouring of your wrath on Jerusalem?" Then he said to me, "The guilt of the house of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. The land is full of blood, and the city full of injustice. For they say, 'The LORD has forsaken the land, and the LORD does not see.' As for me, my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity; I will bring their deeds upon their heads." And behold, the man clothed in linen, with the writing case at his waist, brought back word, saying, "I have done as you commanded me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, "Ah, Lord GOD! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel in the outpouring of your wrath on Jerusalem?"

Ezekiel is left alone in the courts full of bodies. And he does what the faithful have always done: he falls down and pleads. Abraham drew near and asked, Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked? (Gen 18:23). Amos cried, O Lord GOD, please forgive! How can Jacob stand? (Amos 7:2).

The prophet who announces judgment is not hard-hearted. He intercedes. God will later say he looked for someone to stand in the breach before me for the land (22:30). Every believer is called to stand in that place for others in prayer.

Then he said to me, "The guilt of the house of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. The land is full of blood, and the city full of injustice. For they say, 'The LORD has forsaken the land, and the LORD does not see.'

As for me, my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity; I will bring their deeds upon their heads."

God answers honestly. The guilt is exceedingly great: blood, injustice, and the proud lie that God does not see. And the judgment is simply their own deeds coming back on their heads.

But notice that God does not rebuke Ezekiel for asking. The question Will you destroy all the remnant? will be answered, gloriously, later in the book. There will be a remnant, a new heart, dry bones living. Intercession is never wasted.

And behold, the man clothed in linen, with the writing case at his waist, brought back word, saying, "I have done as you commanded me."

The chapter ends not with the executioners' report but with the report of the man who marked the faithful. I have done as you commanded me. Every one of God's people has been marked. None was missed.

That is a picture of our great High Priest, who could say to his Father, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). The one who marks God's people does not fail to finish his work.

9.title: The Mark on the Foreheads
9.overview:
God calls for the executioners of Jerusalem. Six men come with weapons, and with them a man clothed in linen carrying a writing case; they stand beside the bronze altar. The glory of God moves from the cherub to the threshold of the temple, and the man in linen is sent through the city to put a mark on the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over its abominations (vv. 1-4).

The others are ordered to strike without pity, beginning at the sanctuary, but to touch no one with the mark. They begin with the elders in front of the temple and fill the courts with the slain. Left alone, Ezekiel falls on his face and asks whether God will destroy all the remnant of Israel. God replies that the guilt of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great, the land full of blood and injustice, and that the people say he does not see; he will bring their deeds on their heads. The man in linen reports that he has done as he was commanded (vv. 5-11).
9.theology:
Before judgment falls, God marks and protects his own (v. 4; Exod 12:13; Rev 7:3; 2 Tim 2:19).

Those God marks are those who grieve over sin (v. 4; Ps 119:136).

Judgment begins at God's house and with its leaders (v. 6; 1 Pet 4:17).

God's judgment is just, even when we cannot see all its reasons (vv. 6, 9-10; Gen 18:25).

God's servants intercede even as judgment falls, and God does not despise their pleading (v. 8; Gen 18:23; Amos 7:2; 22:30).

The priestly figure who marks the faithful and completes his task points to Christ, who seals his people by the Spirit and finished the work the Father gave him (vv. 2, 11; Eph 1:13; John 17:4).
9.examples:
God's loud cry answering the people's too-late cry.

A scribe's pen walking ahead of six swords.

A mark on the forehead of everyone who grieves.

Judgment starting at the altar.

A prophet alone among the dead, still praying.

I have done as you commanded me.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I looked, and behold, on the expanse that was over the heads of the cherubim there appeared above them something like a sapphire, in appearance like a throne.<sup>2</sup>And he said to the man clothed in linen, "Go in among the whirling wheels underneath the cherubim. Fill your hands with burning coals from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city." And he went in before my eyes.<sup>3</sup>Now the cherubim were standing on the south side of the house, when the man went in, and a cloud filled the inner court.<sup>4</sup>And the glory of the LORD went up from the cherub to the threshold of the house, and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And the sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God Almighty when he speaks.<sup>6</sup>And when he commanded the man clothed in linen, "Take fire from between the whirling wheels, from between the cherubim," he went in and stood beside a wheel.<sup>7</sup>And a cherub stretched out his hand from between the cherubim to the fire that was between the cherubim, and took some of it and put it into the hands of the man clothed in linen, who took it and went out.<sup>8</sup>The cherubim appeared to have the form of a human hand under their wings.<sup>9</sup>And I looked, and behold, there were four wheels beside the cherubim, one beside each cherub, and the appearance of the wheels was like sparkling beryl.<sup>10</sup>And as for their appearance, the four had the same likeness, as if a wheel were within a wheel.<sup>11</sup>When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went, but in whatever direction the front wheel faced, the others followed without turning as they went.<sup>12</sup>And their whole body, their rims, and their spokes, their wings, and the wheels were full of eyes all around—the wheels that the four of them had.<sup>13</sup>As for the wheels, they were called in my hearing "the whirling wheels."<sup>14</sup>And every one had four faces: the first face was the face of the cherub, and the second face was a human face, and the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle.<sup>15</sup>And the cherubim mounted up. These were the living creatures that I saw by the Chebar canal.<sup>16</sup>And when the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them. And when the cherubim lifted up their wings to mount up from the earth, the wheels did not turn from beside them.<sup>17</sup>When they stood still, these stood still, and when they mounted up, these mounted up with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in them.<sup>18</sup>Then the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubim.<sup>19</sup>And the cherubim lifted up their wings and mounted up from the earth before my eyes as they went out, with the wheels beside them. And they stood at the entrance of the east gate of the house of the LORD, and the glory of the God of Israel was over them.<sup>20</sup>These were the living creatures that I saw underneath the God of Israel by the Chebar canal; and I knew that they were cherubim.<sup>21</sup>Each had four faces, and each four wings, and underneath their wings the likeness of human hands.<sup>22</sup>And as for the likeness of their faces, they were the same faces whose appearance I had seen by the Chebar canal. Each one of them went straight forward.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Coals of Fire over the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Above the cherubim appears a throne like sapphire (v. 1). The man clothed in linen is told to take burning coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city (v. 2). A cloud fills the inner court, and the glory of the LORD rises to the threshold, filling the court with brightness while the cherubim's wings sound like the voice of God Almighty when he speaks (vv. 3-5). A cherub puts fire into the man's hands, and he goes out (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The fire of God's holy presence, which should have purified his people, now falls on them in judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, on the expanse that was over the heads of the cherubim there appeared above them something like a sapphire, in appearance like a throne. And he said to the man clothed in linen, "Go in among the whirling wheels underneath the cherubim. Fill your hands with burning coals from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city." And he went in before my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I looked, and behold, on the expanse that was over the heads of the cherubim there appeared above them something like a sapphire, in appearance like a throne.

The vision of chapter 1 is here, in the temple courts: the expanse, the throne like sapphire (the ESV notes, "lapis lazuli"). Now Ezekiel calls the creatures cherubim. The throne that met him in Babylon is the throne of the Most Holy Place.

And he said to the man clothed in linen, "Go in among the whirling wheels underneath the cherubim. Fill your hands with burning coals from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city." And he went in before my eyes.

The same man who marked the faithful in chapter 9 is now sent with fire. He fills his hands with burning coals from between the cherubim — fire from the very presence of God — and scatters them over Jerusalem.

Remember Isaiah's vision. A seraph took a burning coal from the altar and touched his lips: your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for (Isa 6:6-7). The same holy fire that cleansed Isaiah now burns Jerusalem. God's holiness is always fire. It will either purify you or consume you. The difference is whether you come to it confessing, as Isaiah did — Woe is me! For I am lost — or with your back turned, as Jerusalem did.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the cherubim were standing on the south side of the house, when the man went in, and a cloud filled the inner court. And the glory of the LORD went up from the cherub to the threshold of the house, and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the LORD. And the sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God Almighty when he speaks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the cherubim were standing on the south side of the house, when the man went in, and a cloud filled the inner court.

And the glory of the LORD went up from the cherub to the threshold of the house, and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the LORD.

The cloud fills the house, and the courtyard shines with the glory. It is like the day Solomon dedicated the temple, when a cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud (1 Kgs 8:10-11).

But this is not a dedication. It is a farewell. The glory is blazing out one last time as it rises from the Most Holy Place to the doorway. The brightest moment in the courts is the moment of leaving.

And the sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God Almighty when he speaks.

The roar carries into the outer court where ordinary worshippers stood. Did anyone hear? The people who said The LORD does not see (9:9) went on with their business while the voice of God Almighty rumbled over their heads.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he commanded the man clothed in linen, "Take fire from between the whirling wheels, from between the cherubim," he went in and stood beside a wheel. And a cherub stretched out his hand from between the cherubim to the fire that was between the cherubim, and took some of it and put it into the hands of the man clothed in linen, who took it and went out. The cherubim appeared to have the form of a human hand under their wings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he commanded the man clothed in linen, "Take fire from between the whirling wheels, from between the cherubim," he went in and stood beside a wheel.

And a cherub stretched out his hand from between the cherubim to the fire that was between the cherubim, and took some of it and put it into the hands of the man clothed in linen, who took it and went out.

The cherubim appeared to have the form of a human hand under their wings.

The details slow down. The man in linen stands beside a wheel. A cherub reaches out a hand, takes fire and places it into the man's hands. It is deliberate and careful. God's judgment is never hasty or careless. Every coal is handed over under his command.

And the one who carries the fire is the same one who carried the pen. The priestly figure who marks for salvation also brings judgment. So with Christ: the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), and the Saviour who seals his people is the Judge who will come.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel sees again the four wheels beside the cherubim, gleaming like beryl, a wheel within a wheel, moving in any direction (vv. 9-11), full of eyes (v. 12), and he hears them called the whirling wheels (v. 13). The four faces are there (v. 14), and he recognises them: These were the living creatures that I saw by the Chebar canal (v. 15). They move and rise together, for the spirit of the living creatures was in them (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The same throne that met the exiles in Babylon now moves out of Jerusalem's temple.

verseByVerse.quote: And I looked, and behold, there were four wheels beside the cherubim, one beside each cherub, and the appearance of the wheels was like sparkling beryl. And as for their appearance, the four had the same likeness, as if a wheel were within a wheel. When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went, but in whatever direction the front wheel faced, the others followed without turning as they went. And their whole body, their rims, and their spokes, their wings, and the wheels were full of eyes all around—the wheels that the four of them had. As for the wheels, they were called in my hearing "the whirling wheels."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I looked, and behold, there were four wheels beside the cherubim, one beside each cherub, and the appearance of the wheels was like sparkling beryl.

And as for their appearance, the four had the same likeness, as if a wheel were within a wheel.

When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went, but in whatever direction the front wheel faced, the others followed without turning as they went.

Ezekiel describes the wheels again, almost word for word as in chapter 1. Why repeat it? Because the point is identity. This is the same throne. The God who came to the exiles is the God who is now leaving Jerusalem. His throne can go anywhere.

And their whole body, their rims, and their spokes, their wings, and the wheels were full of eyes all around—the wheels that the four of them had.

Now it is not only the rims but the whole body that is covered with eyes. (The ESV notes an alternative: "their whole body, their backs, their hands, and their wings".) Everything around the throne sees. The elders in the dark room said God does not see (8:12). The throne leaving their temple is covered with eyes.

As for the wheels, they were called in my hearing "the whirling wheels."

The name itself suggests motion. The throne of God is not a fixed monument. It is on the move.

verseByVerse.quote: And every one had four faces: the first face was the face of the cherub, and the second face was a human face, and the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle. And the cherubim mounted up. These were the living creatures that I saw by the Chebar canal. And when the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them. And when the cherubim lifted up their wings to mount up from the earth, the wheels did not turn from beside them. When they stood still, these stood still, and when they mounted up, these mounted up with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And every one had four faces: the first face was the face of the cherub, and the second face was a human face, and the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle.

In chapter 1 the four faces were man, lion, ox and eagle (1:10). Here the face of the cherub stands where the ox was. The text does not explain the difference, and Ezekiel insists they are the same faces he saw before (v. 22). What matters to him is recognition, not a catalogue.

And the cherubim mounted up. These were the living creatures that I saw by the Chebar canal.

And when the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them. And when the cherubim lifted up their wings to mount up from the earth, the wheels did not turn from beside them.

When they stood still, these stood still, and when they mounted up, these mounted up with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in them.

The cherubim mounted up — they are rising, ready to leave. And again the perfect unity of the throne: creatures and wheels move as one, because one spirit drives them (the ESV notes, "spirit of life"). There is no confusion in heaven's departure. It is orderly, deliberate and final.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubim (v. 18). The cherubim rise and stop at the east gate of the house of the LORD, with the glory over them (v. 19). Ezekiel knows now what he saw by the Chebar canal: I knew that they were cherubim (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: God's presence does not leave his people in one abrupt moment, but step by step, giving time to repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubim. And the cherubim lifted up their wings and mounted up from the earth before my eyes as they went out, with the wheels beside them. And they stood at the entrance of the east gate of the house of the LORD, and the glory of the God of Israel was over them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubim.

Here is a sentence of heartbreak: the glory of the LORD went out.

Trace the steps. In 9:3 the glory moved from the cherub to the threshold. In 10:4 it rose to the threshold again, filling the court. Now it leaves the threshold and mounts the throne-chariot. In 11:23 it will leave the city altogether. God does not slam the door. He leaves step by step, pausing at each stage, as if waiting for someone to call him back.

Hosea heard God say, I will return again to my place, until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face (Hos 5:15). God's withdrawal is not abandonment; it is a summons to repentance.

And the cherubim lifted up their wings and mounted up from the earth before my eyes as they went out, with the wheels beside them. And they stood at the entrance of the east gate of the house of the LORD, and the glory of the God of Israel was over them.

They pause again, at the east gate, facing the Mount of Olives and the rising sun. It is the gate through which the glory will one day return: the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east (43:2).

Centuries before, when the ark was captured by the Philistines, a dying mother named her son Ichabod, saying The glory has departed from Israel! (1 Sam 4:21). Now it is happening again, not because an enemy took it, but because God's own people drove it out. Six centuries later Jesus stood in the rebuilt temple and said, See, your house is left to you desolate, and Jesus left the temple and was going away (Matt 23:38; 24:1).

verseByVerse.quote: These were the living creatures that I saw underneath the God of Israel by the Chebar canal; and I knew that they were cherubim. Each had four faces, and each four wings, and underneath their wings the likeness of human hands. And as for the likeness of their faces, they were the same faces whose appearance I had seen by the Chebar canal. Each one of them went straight forward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These were the living creatures that I saw underneath the God of Israel by the Chebar canal; and I knew that they were cherubim.

Each had four faces, and each four wings, and underneath their wings the likeness of human hands.

And as for the likeness of their faces, they were the same faces whose appearance I had seen by the Chebar canal. Each one of them went straight forward.

Ezekiel says it with the force of a discovery: I knew that they were cherubim. The beings he met by the canal were the guardians of God's own throne in the Most Holy Place.

For the exiles this was both devastating and wonderful. Devastating, because the glory was leaving Jerusalem. Wonderful, because it had already come to them. The throne that left the temple was the same throne that stood by the Chebar canal. God had not abandoned his people; he had gone with them into exile.

That is still true. God is not tied to a building. Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them (Matt 18:20). And in the end the whole creation will be his dwelling: I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev 21:22).

10.title: The Glory at the Threshold
10.overview:
Ezekiel sees a throne like sapphire above the cherubim. The man clothed in linen is told to fill his hands with burning coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city. A cloud fills the inner court, the glory of the LORD rises to the threshold, the court shines with its brightness, and the sound of the cherubim's wings is like the voice of God Almighty. A cherub hands fire to the man in linen, and he goes out (vv. 1-8).

Ezekiel describes again the wheels beside the cherubim, gleaming like beryl, a wheel within a wheel, moving in every direction and full of eyes, called the whirling wheels. Each creature has four faces. He recognises them as the living creatures he saw by the Chebar canal, and wheels and cherubim rise together as one (vv. 9-17).

Then the glory of the LORD goes out from the threshold of the temple and stands over the cherubim, which rise and stop at the east gate of the house of the LORD with the glory over them. Ezekiel knows now that the living creatures he saw by the canal were cherubim (vv. 18-22).
10.theology:
God's holy fire either cleanses those who come confessing or consumes those who refuse him (vv. 2, 7; Isa 6:6-7).

God's presence can depart from a place of worship that has been given over to idols (vv. 4, 18-19; 1 Sam 4:21-22; Matt 23:38).

God's withdrawal is gradual and deliberate, a summons to repentance rather than a sudden abandonment (vv. 4, 18-19; Hos 5:15).

God sees everything, and his throne is not bound to any building (vv. 12, 16-17, 20-22).

The God who leaves Jerusalem has already come to his people in exile; he goes with them (vv. 15, 20-22; Matt 18:20; Rev 21:22).

The priestly figure who marks for salvation also carries the fire of judgment, pointing to Christ, to whom all judgment is given (vv. 2, 7; John 5:22).
10.examples:
The same coal that cleansed Isaiah's lips, scattered over a city.

The brightest moment in the courts is the moment of leaving.

The voice of God Almighty rumbling over people who did not look up.

Wheels whose whole body is covered in eyes.

A glory that pauses at every doorway.

The same throne by the canal and in the temple.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Cauldron and the Meat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the east gate are twenty-five leaders who give wicked counsel (vv. 1-2), saying This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat — safe inside the walls (v. 3). God, who knows their thoughts, answers that the only meat in the pot is the people they have killed; they themselves will be dragged out and judged by the sword at the border of Israel (vv. 4-12). As Ezekiel prophesies, Pelatiah dies, and Ezekiel cries, Ah, Lord GOD! Will you make a full end of the remnant of Israel? (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who feel safe in their privileged position while oppressing others will find no shelter in it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit lifted me up and brought me to the east gate of the house of the LORD, which faces east. And behold, at the entrance of the gateway there were twenty-five men. And I saw among them Jaazaniah the son of Azzur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people. And he said to me, "Son of man, these are the men who devise iniquity and who give wicked counsel in this city; who say, 'The time is not near to build houses. This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat.' Therefore prophesy against them; prophesy, O son of man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit lifted me up and brought me to the east gate of the house of the LORD, which faces east. And behold, at the entrance of the gateway there were twenty-five men. And I saw among them Jaazaniah the son of Azzur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people.

The glory has paused at the east gate (10:19), and that is where Ezekiel is taken. There he sees twenty-five of Jerusalem's leaders, princes of the people, two of them named. (This Jaazaniah is the son of Azzur, a different man from the Jaazaniah of 8:11.)

And he said to me, "Son of man, these are the men who devise iniquity and who give wicked counsel in this city;

Who devise iniquity and who give wicked counsel. Their sin is not only what they do but what they advise. Leaders shape a whole city by the counsel they give, and these men were steering Jerusalem toward disaster with confident talk. The first psalm begins by blessing the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked (Ps 1:1). Be careful whose counsel you take, and more careful still about the counsel you give.

who say, 'The time is not near to build houses. This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat.'

Here is their slogan. The first part is uncertain: the ESV notes that it may be a question, "Is not the time near...?" But the second part is clear: This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat.

Think what they mean. A cooking pot protects the meat inside from the fire. The walls of Jerusalem are the pot; they, the ruling class who stayed behind, are the choice cuts. The exiles were the scraps thrown away. We are the ones who matter, and we are safe.

God had already said the opposite through Jeremiah. In the vision of two baskets of figs, Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, and the ones who stayed in Jerusalem were the rotten figs (Jer 24:5). The people who felt most secure were the ones in the most danger.

Therefore prophesy against them; prophesy, O son of man."

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit of the LORD fell upon me, and he said to me, "Say, Thus says the LORD: So you think, O house of Israel. For I know the things that come into your mind. You have multiplied your slain in this city and have filled its streets with the slain. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Your slain whom you have laid in the midst of it, they are the meat, and this city is the cauldron, but you shall be brought out of the midst of it. You have feared the sword, and I will bring the sword upon you, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Spirit of the LORD fell upon me, and he said to me, "Say, Thus says the LORD: So you think, O house of Israel. For I know the things that come into your mind.

I know the things that come into your mind. They had not said all this in public. God answers what they thought. Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether (Ps 139:4).

You have multiplied your slain in this city and have filled its streets with the slain.

Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Your slain whom you have laid in the midst of it, they are the meat, and this city is the cauldron, but you shall be brought out of the midst of it.

God turns their proverb inside out. Yes, the city is a cauldron — but the meat in it is the people you murdered. Their corrupt leadership had filled the streets with victims of injustice. Those victims are the only ones who will stay in the pot. You will not be kept safe inside; you will be dragged out.

You have feared the sword, and I will bring the sword upon you, declares the Lord GOD.

They trusted the walls because they feared Babylon's sword. The thing they feared is the thing that will come. Security built on injustice always fails.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will bring you out of the midst of it, and give you into the hands of foreigners, and execute judgments upon you. You shall fall by the sword. I will judge you at the border of Israel, and you shall know that I am the LORD. This city shall not be your cauldron, nor shall you be the meat in the midst of it. I will judge you at the border of Israel, and you shall know that I am the LORD. For you have not walked in my statutes, nor obeyed my rules, but have acted according to the rules of the nations that are around you." And it came to pass, while I was prophesying, that Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died. Then I fell down on my face and cried out with a loud voice and said, "Ah, Lord GOD! Will you make a full end of the remnant of Israel?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I will bring you out of the midst of it, and give you into the hands of foreigners, and execute judgments upon you.

You shall fall by the sword. I will judge you at the border of Israel, and you shall know that I am the LORD.

This city shall not be your cauldron, nor shall you be the meat in the midst of it. I will judge you at the border of Israel,

and you shall know that I am the LORD. For you have not walked in my statutes, nor obeyed my rules, but have acted according to the rules of the nations that are around you."

Notice the irony of give you into the hands of foreigners. These were the men who looked down on the exiles as people cast far from the LORD (v. 15). They will end as captives in foreign hands themselves. God has a way of bringing the proud down to the very place they despised.

At the border of Israel. This came true exactly. When Jerusalem fell, the captain of the guard took the city's leading men to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath (2 Kgs 25:20-21) — at the northern border. They were not killed in the city they thought would protect them. They were led out and executed at the edge of the land.

And the charge: they had lived by the rules of the nations. God's people had adopted the values of the world around them — power, wealth, violence — while keeping the name of God's city.

And it came to pass, while I was prophesying, that Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died. Then I fell down on my face and cried out with a loud voice and said, "Ah, Lord GOD! Will you make a full end of the remnant of Israel?"

In the middle of the sermon, one of the named leaders drops dead. It is proof that the word is not empty. And Ezekiel's reaction is not triumph. He falls on his face and cries out, as he did in 9:8. If even the leaders are dying, will anyone be left?

That is the right heart for anyone who sees God's judgment fall on others. Not satisfaction, but a cry for mercy. And God's answer to Ezekiel's question is the rest of this chapter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — A Sanctuary for a While, and a New Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people left in Jerusalem sneer that the exiles are far from the LORD and the land is theirs (vv. 14-15). But God says to the exiles, I have been a sanctuary to them for a while in the countries where they have gone (v. 16). He will gather them and give them the land (vv. 17-18), And I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they walk in his ways and are his people (vv. 19-20).
verseByVerse.theology: God is present with his scattered people, and he promises the inward renewal that alone makes obedience possible.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, your brothers, even your brothers, your kinsmen, the whole house of Israel, all of them, are those of whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem have said, 'Go far from the LORD; to us this land is given for a possession.' Therefore say, 'Thus says the Lord GOD: Though I removed them far off among the nations, and though I scattered them among the countries, yet I have been a sanctuary to them for a while in the countries where they have gone.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the word of the LORD came to me:

"Son of man, your brothers, even your brothers, your kinsmen, the whole house of Israel, all of them, are those of whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem have said, 'Go far from the LORD; to us this land is given for a possession.'

Ezekiel has asked whether the remnant will perish. God points him to a remnant he had not been thinking about: his fellow exiles. Your brothers, even your brothers, your kinsmen. The ESV notes that kinsmen is literally "the men of your redemption" — the relatives who had the family duty to redeem one another.

The people in Jerusalem looked down on them: Go far from the LORD; to us this land is given. The exiles, they said, had been thrown out of God's presence; the land and God belonged to those who stayed.

It is an old temptation for religious people to decide who is near to God by who is in the right place, the right building, the right group. God sees otherwise.

Therefore say, 'Thus says the Lord GOD: Though I removed them far off among the nations, and though I scattered them among the countries, yet I have been a sanctuary to them for a while in the countries where they have gone.'

This is a sweet verse for exiles. The exiles had no temple. They were far from Jerusalem. And God says: I have been a sanctuary to them. Not a building — God himself was their sanctuary. The ESV notes that for a while may be "in small measure". Even a small measure of God's presence was more than the whole temple once the glory had left it.

This is the heart of the New Testament hope. God's dwelling is not a place but a person. Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them (Matt 18:20). And in the new creation, I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev 21:22). If you are far from where you think you should be, cut off from the church you knew or the home you loved, God himself can be your sanctuary there.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore say, 'Thus says the Lord GOD: I will gather you from the peoples and assemble you out of the countries where you have been scattered, and I will give you the land of Israel.' And when they come there, they will remove from it all its detestable things and all its abominations. And I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, that they may walk in my statutes and keep my rules and obey them. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore say, 'Thus says the Lord GOD: I will gather you from the peoples and assemble you out of the countries where you have been scattered, and I will give you the land of Israel.'

The people in Jerusalem claimed the land. God gives it back to the exiles. The scattered will be gathered.

And when they come there, they will remove from it all its detestable things and all its abominations.

The idols of chapter 8 will be cleared out — by the returning people themselves. Restoration is not simply going home. It is going home changed.

And I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh,

Here is the answer to everything chapters 1-11 have exposed. The problem was never only the idols in the temple. It was the idols in the heart (14:3) — a heart of stone, hard, cold, unmoved by God's word no matter how many prophets he sent.

God does not promise to soften it a little. He promises surgery: I will remove the heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh — a heart that is alive, that feels, that responds to him. And one heart, undivided, no longer split between God and idols. And a new spirit. Chapter 36 will say more: I will put my Spirit within you (36:27).

This is the new birth. Jeremiah promised the same: I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever (Jer 32:39). Paul says the Spirit writes God's word not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts (2 Cor 3:3). God saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5).

that they may walk in my statutes and keep my rules and obey them. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.

Notice the order: new heart first, then obedience — that they may walk. God does not say, Obey me and I will give you a new heart. He gives the new heart so that they can obey. That is grace. And the goal is the oldest promise in the covenant: they shall be my people, and I will be their God.

If you find your heart hard toward God, do not wait until you have softened it yourself. Ask him to do what he promised.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — The Glory Leaves the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who cling to their idols will receive their deeds on their heads (v. 21). Then the cherubim lift their wings, And the glory of the LORD went up from the midst of the city and stood on the mountain that is on the east side of the city (vv. 22-23). Ezekiel is carried back to the exiles in Chaldea, and he tells them everything the LORD had shown him (vv. 24-25).
verseByVerse.theology: When God's presence leaves a city, it is the end of its protection, but not the end of his purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for those whose heart goes after their detestable things and their abominations, I will bring their deeds upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD." Then the cherubim lifted up their wings, with the wheels beside them, and the glory of the God of Israel was over them. And the glory of the LORD went up from the midst of the city and stood on the mountain that is on the east side of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for those whose heart goes after their detestable things and their abominations, I will bring their deeds upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD."

The promise does not cancel the warning. Those whose hearts keep chasing their idols will receive what their deeds deserve. The new heart is offered; it is not forced on those who love their old one.

Then the cherubim lifted up their wings, with the wheels beside them, and the glory of the God of Israel was over them.

And the glory of the LORD went up from the midst of the city and stood on the mountain that is on the east side of the city.

The last stage. The glory leaves not just the temple but the city, and stops on the mountain to the east — the Mount of Olives, that lies before Jerusalem on the east (Zech 14:4). It pauses there, looking back over the city, one last time.

Hold that picture beside the Gospels. After Jesus told the leaders of Jerusalem your house is left to you desolate, he left the temple and sat on the Mount of Olives (Matt 23:38; 24:1, 3). Coming down that same mountain a few days earlier, he saw the city and wept over it (Luke 19:41). And from that mountain he ascended, with the promise that he will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven (Acts 1:11-12). The glory that left Jerusalem in Ezekiel's vision walked its streets in the flesh — and it will return.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit lifted me up and brought me in the vision by the Spirit of God into Chaldea, to the exiles. Then the vision that I had seen went up from me. And I told the exiles all the things that the LORD had shown me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Spirit lifted me up and brought me in the vision by the Spirit of God into Chaldea, to the exiles. Then the vision that I had seen went up from me.

And I told the exiles all the things that the LORD had shown me.

The vision ends, and Ezekiel is back in his house in Babylon, with the elders still sitting in front of him (8:1). And he tells them all the things that the LORD had shown me — the idols, the executioners, the departing glory, and the promise of a new heart.

That is the task of every faithful messenger: to tell all of it. The hard parts and the hopeful parts. The glory leaving, and the God who is a sanctuary in exile. The heart of stone, and the heart of flesh.

11.title: A New Heart and a Departing Glory
11.overview:
At the east gate of the temple Ezekiel sees twenty-five leaders, among them Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, who give wicked counsel and say that the city is a cauldron and they are the meat, safe inside. God, who knows their thoughts, declares that the only meat in the pot is those they have killed; they will be brought out, given to foreigners and judged by the sword at the border of Israel, because they have lived by the rules of the nations. As Ezekiel prophesies, Pelatiah dies, and Ezekiel falls on his face asking if God will make a full end of the remnant (vv. 1-13).

God answers that the people of Jerusalem have written off the exiles as far from the LORD, but he has been a sanctuary to the exiles in the lands where they are scattered. He will gather them, give them the land, and they will remove its idols. He will give them one heart and a new spirit, take away the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh, so that they walk in his statutes and are his people and he their God. Those whose hearts go after idols will receive their deeds on their heads (vv. 14-21).

The cherubim rise, and the glory of the LORD goes up from the city and stands on the mountain east of it. The Spirit brings Ezekiel back to the exiles in Chaldea, and he tells them everything the LORD showed him (vv. 22-25).
11.theology:
Privilege and position are no protection for those who oppress others; God judges by the heart and the deeds (vv. 2-12; 2 Kgs 25:20-21).

God knows every thought (v. 5; Ps 139:4).

God's people are not defined by location; he himself is the sanctuary of his scattered people (v. 16; Matt 18:20; Rev 21:22).

The root problem is the heart, and God promises to replace the heart of stone with a heart of flesh and to give a new spirit; obedience follows the gift (vv. 19-20; 36:25-27; Jer 32:39; 2 Cor 3:3; Titus 3:5).

The promise of renewal does not cancel judgment on those who cling to idols (v. 21).

The glory that left Jerusalem for the mountain east of the city came back in Jesus, who wept over the city from that mountain, ascended from it, and will return (vv. 22-23; Luke 19:41; Acts 1:11-12).
11.examples:
Leaders who think they are the prime cuts in a safe pot.

A proverb turned inside out: the only meat is your victims.

A man dropping dead in the middle of the sermon.

God himself as a sanctuary in a foreign country.

Heart surgery: stone out, flesh in.

The glory pausing on the Mount of Olives to look back.
